title: Basic async
summary: Callbacks, timers, promises and async/await: how code that finishes later is scheduled, ordered and made to handle errors.

misconceptions.description: Believes setTimeout makes the program wait for the delay, so the lines below it run only after the callback.
Believes a delay of 0 makes the callback run immediately, before the next line.
Believes writing a call such as fn() where a callback is expected still schedules the function for later.
Believes timers fire in the order they were written instead of the order of their delays.
Reads a value from another step of the run, or forgets what earlier calls left behind, instead of the value at the step asked about.
Believes a then handler, or the code after await, runs at once even when the promise is already settled.
Believes the value a handler returns is lost or replaced by the earlier value instead of reaching the next link.
Believes the chain stops after a catch, so later then handlers never run.
Believes an async function behaves like a normal one: its value comes back directly and a throw escapes at the call.
Believes await freezes the whole program, so other code waits until the promise settles.
Believes a call to an async function gives the final value without await.
Believes a try/catch also covers a rejection that happens after the try block has finished, when there is no await.
Believes finally does not run after catch has handled an error.
Believes the lines after a failing await inside try still run before catch.

conceptCard.title: A function you hand over to be called later
conceptCard.body: A callback is a function you hand to other code, which calls it later. setTimeout(callback, delay) schedules the callback after the delay in milliseconds and returns at once, so the lines below it run first. Pass the function itself, not a call to it.

conceptCard.title: A value that arrives later
conceptCard.body: A promise stands for a value that arrives later. then(handler) runs when it is fulfilled, and catch(handler) runs when it is rejected. Both return a new promise, so calls chain, and each handler passes its returned value to the next one. Handlers run after the current code finishes.

conceptCard.title: Pausing inside a function
conceptCard.body: An async function always returns a promise. Inside it, await pauses that function until a promise settles, then gives back the value. Only the async function waits: the code that called it keeps running.

conceptCard.title: Catching a rejection
conceptCard.body: When an awaited promise rejects, await throws, so a try/catch around it works. finally runs afterwards in every case. Without await, try/catch cannot see a rejection that happens later: attach .catch() to the promise instead.

items.prompt: Three dishes are scheduled with different delays. What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. menu prints at once. The timers then fire by delay: 100, 200, 300.
That follows the order of the lines. Timers fire by their delay, not by where they were written.
setTimeout does not hold up the program. The line say('menu') does not wait for any timer.

items.explanation: setTimeout returns at once, so the plain call prints menu first. The three callbacks wait in a queue ordered by delay: salad at 100, bread at 200, soup at 300.
hints: Which line is not inside a setTimeout?
A timer callback runs after its delay, and the delay decides the order, not the line number.
Print the plain call first, then sort the three dishes by their numbers.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Which statement explains the order in which this code prints?

options.text: The callback waits until the rest of the code has finished, even with a delay of 0.
options.feedback: Right. A timer callback never interrupts the running code, whatever its delay.

options.text: A delay of 0 makes the callback run immediately, so rest prints second.
options.feedback: A delay of 0 is a request to run as soon as possible, after the current code. It is not a direct call.

options.text: setTimeout holds back the lines below it until its callback has run, so rest prints second.
options.feedback: The lines below setTimeout do not wait. The call returns at once and the program goes on.

items.explanation: setTimeout only schedules the callback. The current code runs to its end first, so reach summit prints before rest, even though the delay is 0.
hints: Compare the order of the lines with the order of the output.
A callback passed to setTimeout runs only when the current code is finished.
Ask whether any line below setTimeout can run before the callback.

items.prompt: Which statement is true about this code?

options.text: catch returns a new promise fulfilled with its handler's value, so the last then prints waitlist.
options.feedback: Right. After a catch handler returns normally, the chain continues as fulfilled.

options.text: After catch has run the chain is finished, so the last then never runs.
options.feedback: catch returns a promise too. When its handler returns a value, the next then runs with that value.

options.text: The last then receives the original error, because catch only observes the rejection.
options.feedback: The value of the next link is what the catch handler returns, here the text waitlist, not the old error.

items.explanation: catch is like then for rejections and also returns a promise. Its handler returns waitlist without throwing, so that promise is fulfilled with waitlist and the last then prints it.
hints: Follow the value from the first line to the last.
Every link in a chain, catch included, returns a new promise.
What does the catch handler return, and who receives it?

options.feedback: Right. await throws the rejection inside try, so catch runs, and finally runs in every case.

options.feedback: finally runs whether or not an error happened and whether or not catch ran.

options.text: await does not stop the try block, so saved prints first and failed after it.

items.prompt: Write the body of checkReadings(readings). Throw an Error inside try when the array is empty and catch it. finally appends '!'. Return 'ok!' or 'empty!'.
items.explanation: The throw jumps to catch, which sets empty. finally runs on both paths and appends the exclamation mark. Without catch the error escapes; without finally the mark is missing. Check the length, not the first element.
hints: Which block runs on both the good path and the error path?
A throw inside try jumps straight to catch; finally runs afterwards.
Set the status in catch and add the mark only in finally.
